bugClass.title: Shared output file overwritten without ownership validation
bugClass.cause: A process writes to a default or shared filesystem path and replaces existing contents without verifying that the file belongs to the same database, instance, or owner. Related status reporting reads a persisted success record rather than validating the current file on disk, so it can report success after the file has been replaced or emptied.
bugClass.criteria: Classify another site when runtime code writes, copies, renames, or atomically replaces a file at a shared or default-derived path without checking the existing file's owner or data identity. Also admit cases where status is derived only from a stored success/state record and does not inspect the artifact it claims is current. Either mechanism is sufficient when it can produce the reported stale or clobbered artifact.

candidates.evidence: Lines 14–21 create a random temporary file, then `rename(temp, path)` replaces the destination without checking its existing owner or data identity. When atomicJson is called for a destination shared across owners or instances, existing contents can be overwritten; the excerpt gives no ownership guard or path scoping.

`trackerNodeRuntime.ts` lines 69–78 assigns active hub backups to `~/backups/tracker/native` by default and a shared external directory at `~/backups/tracker`, unless `backupDirectory` is configured. This establishes a default-derived backup location without ownership validation in the excerpt; the hub trigger is explicit, while only live backup writes are described.

Lines 115–116 write a report to `resolve(root, report.file)` through a random temporary file and rename it over the target, without visible ownership or identity validation. The excerpt does not show whether `root`/`report.file` is a shared or default-derived path, so the class trigger is incomplete.

Lines 50–56 save encrypted state by writing a temporary file and renaming it over `config.file`, with no visible check of the existing file's owner or identity. The excerpt does not establish that this configured path is shared or default-derived.

Lines 20–23 write a staged tracker bundle record and rename it over the record path without validating the existing file's identity. The excerpt does not establish whether `file` is shared/default-derived or whether overwriting can clobber another owner's artifact.

Lines 29–32 save state by writing a PID-named temporary file and renaming it over `this.path` without checking the existing file's owner or identity. The excerpt does not show whether the state path is shared/default-derived; the separate exclusive lock only scopes `run`, and its use around `save` is not established here.

Lines 48–59 restore files into a directory derived from the record's commit and start time, writing each file directly and atomically replacing `record.json`. The excerpt does not show whether that directory is unique to the same record or whether existing file ownership/data identity is validated, so shared-path clobbering is not established.

Lines 33–42 serialize adapter state to its configured `this.file` through a unique temporary file and rename. The excerpt does not establish whether the configured path is shared across owners or whether the serialized value is tied to a database/instance, so the required trigger is unclear.

Lines 36–47 read current cooldowns, update one provider, then write a PID-specific temporary file and rename it over the root-derived cooldown file. This may replace data without a visible ownership check, but the excerpt does not show the path derivation or whether separate owners share that root; the triggering shared-path condition is unestablished.

Lines 15–21 write benchmark JSON to either an explicitly supplied path or a profile-derived path, without a visible existing-file identity check. The excerpt does not establish that either path is shared across unrelated owners or that replacing an artifact can create the reported stale-status behavior.

`trackerBackupState.ts` line 36 reads state, merges changes, writes `${path}.tmp`, then renames it over `path`. This can replace an existing state file without checking its owner or database identity, but the excerpt does not establish that `path` is shared/default-derived or that this clobbers the reported backup artifact.

Lines 45–52 write a scenario manifest directly to a root-relative path derived from `manifest.id`, without an existing-file identity check. The excerpt does not establish that IDs can collide across owners or that the path is shared across databases or instances.

Lines 11–23 read and modify a `package.json`, then write the updated contents to the same path without an identity check. The excerpt does not establish that the path is shared across owners or databases, nor does it show stale status reporting.
